options.a: Escalation to the appropriate level of authority.
options.b: Closure of the risk.
options.c: Assessment of probability.
options.d: Baselining the schedule.

questions.explanation: Escalation follows directly from the definition of an issue as a problem beyond the project manager's delegated authority.

questions.stem: What is assessed once an issue has been logged?

options.a: Its probability of occurring.
options.b: Its severity and consequence for objectives.
options.c: Its float.
options.d: Its configuration status.

questions.explanation: The event is certain, so there is no probability to assess. Severity and consequence are what determine the response.

questions.stem: What happens after an issue has been resolved?

options.a: It is removed from all records.
options.b: It is escalated to the sponsor for information only.
options.c: It is closed, and any consequences are reflected in the plan, baseline or risk register.
options.d: It is converted back into a risk.

questions.explanation: Closing without updating the plan leaves the project reporting against a picture that the issue has already changed.

questions.stem: Why is an issue logged rather than simply discussed?

options.a: So that it exists as a recorded item with an owner and can be tracked to closure.
options.b: Because logging reduces its severity.
options.c: Because unlogged issues cannot be escalated.
options.d: Because the governance board audits all conversations.

questions.explanation: A recorded item can be tracked. An escalating conversation cannot.

questions.stem: A component meets its specification exactly and cost very little. In quality terms, what is it?

options.a: High quality, because it is fit for purpose.
options.b: Quality cannot be judged without stakeholder opinion.
options.c: Low quality, because it exceeds nothing.
options.d: Low quality, because it was cheap.

questions.explanation: Quality is measured against agreed requirements, not against expense or luxury.

questions.stem: A team adds extra features beyond the agreed specification. What has happened?

options.a: Unapproved scope has been added, which is a change control matter.
options.b: Quality has been improved.
options.c: The acceptance criteria have been met early.
options.d: Benefits have been realised.

questions.explanation: Gold plating is not higher quality. It is scope that nobody assessed, priced or approved.

questions.stem: What does the definition of quality cover besides outputs?

options.a: Stakeholders.
options.b: Budgets.
options.c: Processes.
options.d: Schedules.

questions.explanation: Covering processes as well as outputs is what allows quality assurance to exist as a separate idea from quality control.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not part of the definition of quality?

options.a: Fitness for purpose.
options.b: Applying to processes as well as outputs.
options.c: Value for money.
options.d: Meeting agreed requirements.

questions.explanation: Value for money is a commercial judgement that belongs to the business case, not to the definition of quality.

questions.stem: Why does quality management cover processes as well as outputs?

options.a: Because processes are cheaper to inspect.
options.b: Because checking only outputs finds defects after the money has been spent producing them.
options.c: Because outputs cannot be measured objectively.
options.d: Because the sponsor requires process reports.

questions.explanation: Managing both catches problems at the point where they are cheapest to fix.

questions.stem: Which of the three quality activities is quality management the umbrella for?

options.a: Request, evaluation and decision.
options.b: Planning, identification and control.
options.c: Identification, analysis and response.
options.d: Planning, assurance and control.

questions.explanation: The other three lists belong to risk management, change control and configuration management.

questions.stem: How does quality management support handover?

options.a: By transferring responsibility to the supplier.
options.b: By closing the risk register.
options.c: By making acceptance a check against agreed criteria rather than an argument.
options.d: By removing the need for user involvement.

questions.explanation: Criteria agreed in advance turn transition into a verification step instead of a negotiation under time pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not the purpose of quality management?

options.a: Providing confidence that requirements will be met.
options.b: Ensuring processes are appropriate.
options.c: Ensuring outputs meet required standards.
options.d: Producing deliverables at the lowest possible cost.

questions.explanation: Cost minimisation is a commercial aim. Quality management is about meeting agreed standards.

questions.stem: When does quality planning take place?

options.a: Early, during definition, before the work is done.
options.b: After each deliverable is produced.
options.c: At the post project review.
options.d: Continuously during deployment only.

questions.explanation: Planning produces the reference that assurance and control both use later. Without it there is nothing to test against.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an output of quality planning?

options.a: Acceptance criteria for each deliverable.
options.b: An audit report on process compliance.
options.c: A record of defects found.
options.d: Test results for a completed component.

questions.explanation: Test results come from control and audit reports from assurance. Planning sets the standard those later activities check against.

questions.stem: Why is agreeing acceptance criteria in advance so valuable?

options.a: Because it removes the need for testing.
options.b: Because criteria cannot be written after work begins.
options.c: Because the sponsor cannot approve the plan otherwise.
options.d: Because criteria agreed later turn handover into a negotiation with the project already spent.

questions.explanation: It is the single most valuable thing quality planning does, and it costs almost nothing at the time.

questions.stem: Where are externally imposed regulatory standards recognised?

options.a: At the benefits review.
options.b: During quality control.
options.c: During quality planning.
options.d: In the risk register only.

questions.explanation: A regulated project inherits standards it does not choose, and planning is where that is caught rather than discovered late.

questions.stem: When does quality control take place?

options.a: Continuously, independently of any output.
options.b: After an output has been produced.
options.c: Before the work begins.
options.d: Only at project closure.

questions.explanation: Control is applied to the thing produced, which means it can only happen once there is something to inspect.

questions.stem: What is the outcome of quality control?

options.a: Confidence that the process is appropriate.
options.b: A decision on whether the project should continue.
options.c: A verdict on whether the output meets its acceptance criteria.
options.d: A set of standards for the project.

questions.explanation: It produces a pass or fail. If it fails, the output is reworked and retested.

questions.stem: Which activity is an example of quality control?

options.a: Auditing whether the team followed the agreed process.
options.b: Deciding which standards the project will apply.
options.c: Testing a software component against its specification.
options.d: Confirming that benefits have been realised.

questions.explanation: Control examines the product. Auditing the process is assurance, and setting standards is planning.

questions.stem: Why is quality control alone insufficient?

options.a: Because control happens before the work.
options.b: Because control cannot detect defects.
options.c: Because an acceptable item can come from a process that will not reliably repeat it.
options.d: Because control is always performed by the supplier.

questions.explanation: Control checks this item. Assurance asks whether the way of working will keep producing acceptable ones.

questions.stem: Who normally carries out quality assurance?

options.a: Someone independent of the team doing the work.
options.b: The supplier's finance department.
options.c: The end users.
options.d: The team producing the deliverable.

questions.explanation: Assurance provided by the people being assured is worth very little, which is why independence matters.

questions.stem: What question does quality assurance answer?

options.a: Have the expected benefits been realised?
options.b: If we keep working this way, will the results be acceptable?
options.c: Should the project continue to the next phase?
options.d: Is this particular item acceptable?

questions.explanation: Assurance is forward looking and about the process. Control is backward looking and about the item.

questions.stem: How does quality assurance support governance?

options.a: It removes the need for a decision gate.
options.b: It sets the project's tolerances.
options.c: It approves changes beyond the project manager's authority.
options.d: It gives a decision gate an independent view of whether the project is being run properly.

questions.explanation: A gate decision based only on the project manager's own report is weaker than one supported by independent assurance.

questions.stem: Which claim about quality assurance is false?

options.a: It guarantees that no defects will occur.
options.b: It provides confidence that requirements will be met.
options.c: It examines processes rather than products.
options.d: It is usually carried out independently.

questions.explanation: Assurance provides confidence about the process. Guarantees about outcomes are not available from any quality activity.

questions.stem: Which review asks whether the expected benefits have actually been realised?

options.a: A project audit.
options.b: A decision gate.
options.c: A post project review.
options.d: A benefit review.

questions.explanation: Benefits emerge over time, so this cannot be answered at closure. It is why extended life cycles exist.

questions.stem: Which review asks whether the project complied with the organisation's processes and standards?

options.a: A project audit.
options.b: A post project review.
options.c: A decision gate.
options.d: A benefit review.

questions.explanation: An audit is a compliance and assurance activity, normally independent, and it can happen at any point.

questions.stem: What is the test applied at a decision gate?

options.a: Whether the deliverable meets its acceptance criteria.
options.b: Whether the risk register is up to date.
options.c: Whether lessons have been captured.
options.d: Whether the business case remains viable given what is now known.

questions.explanation: Gates are why a project that has stopped being worth doing can be stopped rather than continuing on momentum.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a post project review and a benefit review?

options.a: They are the same review at different times.
options.b: One looks at how the project was managed; the other at whether the results were worth having.
options.c: One applies to linear projects and the other to iterative.
options.d: One is internal and the other external.

questions.explanation: These two are the most confused pair in the outcome, and the exam offers both as options for either question.

questions.stem: A project manager issues a detailed weekly report that nobody opens. Has communication taken place?

options.a: No, because information has been transmitted but not understood.
options.b: Yes, because the information was accurate.
options.c: Yes, because the report was distributed on schedule.
options.d: No, because the report was too detailed.

questions.explanation: Sending is transmission. It becomes communication only once it has been received and understood as intended.

questions.stem: Why does the definition of communication include the word exchange?

options.a: Because reports must be exchanged for approval.
options.b: Because information has commercial value.
options.c: Because communication runs in both directions.
options.d: Because two methods must always be used.

questions.explanation: A project manager who issues reports and receives nothing back has a broadcast, and broadcasts hide unhappy stakeholders.

questions.stem: How can a project manager confirm shared understanding has been reached?

options.a: By asking the other party to say what they have understood.
options.b: By recording the message in the project file.
options.c: By copying in the sponsor.
options.d: By sending the message a second time.

questions.explanation: Confirmation is the mechanism that closes the loop. Noticing that someone's questions imply a different picture works too.

questions.stem: Besides status information, what else does project communication cover?

options.a: Only written records for audit purposes.
options.b: Building relationships, managing expectations and reaching agreement.
options.c: Only communication with the project team.
options.d: Only formal reporting to the governance board.

questions.explanation: That breadth is what connects communication to stakeholder engagement and to leadership.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of physical, written communication?

options.a: It is the cheapest way to reach a dispersed team.
options.b: It provides immediate feedback.
options.c: It produces a durable and accurate record that everyone receives in identical form.
options.d: It allows body language to be observed.

questions.explanation: The record and the identical form are its strengths. Body language and immediate feedback belong to face to face.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of virtual communication?

options.a: It never depends on technology.
options.b: It conveys tone and body language most completely.
options.c: It reaches people wherever they are, making dispersed teams workable.
options.d: It removes the need for a communication plan.

questions.explanation: Reach is what virtual buys. Richness of signal is what it trades away.

questions.stem: For which situation is face to face communication normally the strongest choice?

options.a: Creating an auditable record of a decision.
options.b: A sensitive or contentious discussion where trust matters.
options.c: Reaching two hundred stakeholders at once.
options.d: Distributing a detailed technical specification.

questions.explanation: Immediate feedback and non-verbal signal make it the best method for anything difficult. The other three play to physical and virtual strengths.

questions.stem: What does a competent communication plan do with the three methods?

options.a: Avoids virtual communication for external stakeholders.
options.b: Selects one method and applies it consistently.
options.c: Uses face to face wherever possible.
options.d: Uses all three, matched to the message rather than to habit.

questions.explanation: Each method trades something. Matching method to message is what the plan is for.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of face to face communication?

options.a: It cannot convey tone.
options.b: It requires reliable technology.
options.c: It normally leaves no record unless someone takes one.
options.d: It provides no immediate feedback.

questions.explanation: What was agreed can be disputed afterwards. It also requires people to be in the same place, which costs time and money.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of physical, written communication?

options.a: It carries no tone, so a neutral message can read as curt.
options.b: It requires all parties to be co-located.
options.c: It leaves no audit trail.
options.d: It cannot convey complex detail.

questions.explanation: It is also slow and largely one way, so a misunderstanding can persist until it surfaces as a problem.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine disadvantage of virtual communication?

options.a: It requires everyone to be in the same room.
options.b: It never leaves a record.
options.c: Non-verbal signals are reduced, so conflict is harder to detect.
options.d: It cannot be used with external stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Technology dependence and reduced signal are the real weaknesses. The other three options are simply untrue.

questions.stem: What general principle governs the choice of communication method?

options.a: The richest method is always the correct one.
options.b: Every method trades something: richness against reach, immediacy against record.
options.c: The method should match the sender's preference.
options.d: The cheapest method should be preferred.

questions.explanation: Recognising the trade is what lets a project manager choose deliberately rather than by habit.

questions.stem: Which of the following belongs in a communication plan?

options.a: The frequency at which each audience receives information.
options.b: The version history of each deliverable.
options.c: The total float on each activity.
options.d: The tolerance limits for issue escalation.

questions.explanation: Audience, content, frequency, method and owner. Anything belonging to another process is not plan content.

questions.stem: What does a communication plan draw on directly?

options.a: The configuration register.
options.b: The work breakdown structure.
options.c: The estimating funnel.
options.d: The stakeholder analysis.

questions.explanation: Analysis identifies who matters and how much influence they hold. The plan turns that into scheduled actions.

questions.stem: Why should a communication plan be revisited during the project?

options.a: Because stakeholders and their information needs change as the project moves through phases.
options.b: Because the governance board requires quarterly reissue.
options.c: Because the plan expires at each decision gate.
options.d: Because communication methods become obsolete.

questions.explanation: A plan written at definition and never revisited describes an audience that has moved on.

questions.stem: Which element of a communication plan creates accountability?

options.a: Setting the frequency.
options.b: Listing the audiences.
options.c: Naming who is responsible for producing and sending each item.
options.d: Recording the method used.

questions.explanation: Without a named owner, communication is everybody's job and therefore nobody's.

questions.stem: What happens to communication in the absence of a plan?

options.a: It becomes the sponsor's responsibility.
options.b: It stops entirely.
options.c: It defaults to whoever asks loudest, neglecting stakeholders who do not chase.
options.d: It is replaced by stakeholder analysis.

questions.explanation: The stakeholders who chase get information, and the ones who matter more but stay quiet are neglected until they become a problem.

questions.stem: How does a communication plan help manage expectations?

options.a: It prevents stakeholders from raising concerns.
options.b: People told what is happening on a predictable schedule are less likely to invent their own version.
options.c: It commits the project to a fixed completion date.
options.d: It transfers expectation management to the PMO.

questions.explanation: Information gaps get filled by speculation. A predictable rhythm removes the gaps.

questions.stem: Why does consistency of message matter most when news is bad?

options.a: Because bad news must be withheld until confirmed.
options.b: Because only the sponsor may deliver bad news.
options.c: Because several versions of bad news damage credibility and spread faster than good news.
options.d: Because bad news requires face to face communication.

questions.explanation: A plan means everyone hears the same message rather than assembling their own from fragments.

questions.stem: What can a communication plan not do?

options.a: Make stakeholders agree with the project's decisions.
options.b: Create accountability for reporting.
options.c: Ensure information reaches the right people.
options.d: Provide a consistent message.

questions.explanation: It ensures the message arrives and is understood. What the recipient does with it is a separate matter.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly separates leadership from management?

options.a: Leadership applies to sponsors; management applies to project managers.
options.b: Leadership sets direction and aligns people; management plans, organises and controls the work.
options.c: They are the same activity described differently.
options.d: Leadership controls the work; management sets the vision.

questions.explanation: They are complementary and a project manager usually does both at once, but they are not the same thing.

questions.stem: Why is leadership through influence particularly important for project managers?

options.a: Because sponsors retain all formal authority.
options.b: Because they frequently lead people who report elsewhere and over whom they have no authority.
options.c: Because influence is faster than instruction.
options.d: Because authority is forbidden in project environments.

questions.explanation: Matrix organisations are the norm, and that is exactly why influence rather than authority sits in the definition.

questions.stem: What does leadership produce that formal authority alone does not?

options.a: A faster reporting line.
options.b: A larger budget.
options.c: Commitment rather than mere compliance.
options.d: A shorter critical path.

questions.explanation: Authority can compel compliance. Influence produces commitment, which is more durable and survives the leader leaving the room.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not part of the definition of leadership?

options.a: Setting direction.
options.b: Aligning others towards a common purpose.
options.c: Establishing vision.
options.d: Holding formal authority over the team.

questions.explanation: Vision, direction, influence and alignment. Authority is the classic trap for anyone equating the two.

questions.stem: Why does clarity of role improve team performance?

options.a: Because it removes the need for a schedule.
options.b: Because it shortens the critical path.
options.c: Because it reduces the number of team members needed.
options.d: Because ambiguity produces both gaps and duplication in the work.

questions.explanation: It is the same problem the responsibility assignment matrix exists to expose, seen from the people side.

questions.stem: Why does a team leader benefit from an environment where bad news can be raised early?

options.a: Because it removes the need for progress reporting.
options.b: Because problems are heard while they are still small enough to fix.
options.c: Because it transfers responsibility to the team.
options.d: Because it reduces the number of problems that occur.

questions.explanation: A team that cannot raise bad news reports green until the week the project fails.

questions.stem: Why does involving a team in decisions improve performance?

options.a: Because decisions are always better with more people.
options.b: Because it reduces the leader's workload.
options.c: Because it satisfies governance requirements.
options.d: Because people support what they helped shape.

questions.explanation: Commitment to a decision is higher when the people executing it had a hand in making it.

questions.stem: Why does a leader's own behaviour matter to team performance?

options.a: Because it decides the resource allocation.
options.b: Because a leader who conceals problems gets a team that conceals problems.
options.c: Because behaviour determines formal authority.
options.d: Because leaders are assessed by the governance board.

questions.explanation: The leader's behaviour sets the actual standard, whatever the stated policy says.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a challenge when leading a project team?

options.a: Stable membership from start to finish.
options.b: A clearly defined responsibility assignment matrix.
options.c: Members reporting to a line manager as well as to the project.
options.d: The team being co-located throughout.

questions.explanation: Matrix reporting divides authority. The other three all make leading a team easier rather than harder.

questions.stem: Why is changing team membership a particular challenge on projects?

options.a: Because the baseline must be re-approved.
options.b: Because the risk register must be rewritten.
options.c: Because the team repeatedly re-forms and can revisit earlier development stages.
options.d: Because new members cost more.

questions.explanation: This connects directly to Tuckman. A team that gains or loses people does not simply continue performing.

questions.stem: Why do dispersed teams create difficulty for a project manager?

options.a: They cannot be given work packages.
options.b: They cannot use virtual communication.
options.c: They require more formal authority.
options.d: Non-verbal signals are reduced, so disengagement and conflict are harder to spot.

questions.explanation: It is the same weakness identified as a disadvantage of virtual communication, seen from the leadership side.

questions.stem: How should a project manager treat conflict within the team?

options.a: Remove the individuals involved.
options.b: Escalate every instance to the sponsor.
options.c: Handle it, since unaddressed conflict does not disappear.
options.d: Avoid it, to protect team morale.

questions.explanation: Conflict arises from competing priorities and resource pressure. Suppressing it pushes it underground where it costs more.

questions.stem: At which Tuckman stage do roles settle, working practices get agreed and trust develops?

options.a: Storming.
options.b: Performing.
options.c: Forming.
options.d: Norming.

questions.explanation: Norming is where the team starts operating as a unit. Performing is the later stage of effective delivery with little intervention.

questions.stem: At which Tuckman stage is the team polite, tentative and unclear about roles?

options.a: Performing.
options.b: Storming.
options.c: Norming.
options.d: Forming.

questions.explanation: Forming is the orientation stage, and the leader is normally directive because nobody yet knows how the team works.

questions.stem: How should a project manager treat the storming stage?

options.a: As a stage to be prevented by restricting discussion.
options.b: As evidence that the wrong people were selected.
options.c: As a reason to escalate to the sponsor.
options.d: As a normal and necessary stage rather than a sign of failure.

questions.explanation: Suppressing storming tends to push the same disagreements underground, where they resurface later and less openly.

questions.stem: Which Belbin role turns ideas into practical action?

options.a: Monitor evaluator.
options.b: Implementer.
options.c: Plant.
options.d: Resource investigator.

questions.explanation: The plant generates the ideas, the implementer delivers them, and the resource investigator looks outside the team for contacts and opportunities.

questions.stem: What practical use does Belbin's model have for a project manager?

options.a: Deciding the team's reporting line.
options.b: Understanding team balance, so work can be allocated to strengths and gaps identified.
options.c: Determining who should be promoted.
options.d: Setting individual performance targets.

questions.explanation: A team of nine idea generators delivers nothing, and a team with none produces nothing new. Balance is the point.

questions.stem: What is the essential difference between Tuckman's model and Belbin's?

options.a: They describe the same thing at different levels of detail.
options.b: Tuckman applies to iterative teams and Belbin to linear ones.
options.c: Tuckman describes stages over time; Belbin describes roles within the team.
options.d: Tuckman is about individuals and Belbin about the group.

questions.explanation: One is time, the other is composition. Both are named in the syllabus, so both are examinable.

questions.stem: Which statement about risk management is false?

options.a: It seeks to minimise threats to objectives.
options.b: It makes uncertainty visible early enough to act cheaply.
options.c: It seeks to maximise opportunities.
options.d: It removes uncertainty so the plan can be relied on.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty is inherent in unique work. It is managed, never removed, and any option promising removal is wrong on principle.

questions.stem: Two risks are recorded. One is near certain and severe, the other remote and trivial. What does this difference come from?

options.a: The response stage, which assigns owners.
options.b: The identification stage, which ranks risks as they are found.
options.c: The closure stage, which removes minor risks.
options.d: The analysis stage, which assesses probability and impact so attention can be prioritised.

questions.explanation: Analysis is what makes prioritisation possible. Identification only finds risks; it does not weigh them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not part of the definition of communication?

options.a: Communication running in both directions.
options.b: Confirmation that understanding is shared.
options.c: Persuading the recipient to agree with the message.
options.d: The exchange of information between parties.

questions.explanation: Persuasion may be a purpose on a given occasion, but it is not what communication means. Agreement is not required for communication to have occurred.
